name: Jibbali
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: The stress in Mehri, Hobyōt, Baṭḥari, Ḥarsūsi is on the last long syllable or on the first syllable if there are only short syllables in the stress unit. Jibbāli is particular in the sense that a word or a stress unit can have several stressed syllables: JL minšérɔ́t (ML mənḳarḗt) 'middle finger'. When a word has only one stress, it is on the same syllable as the Mehri word: JL mišəndɔ́t (ML məkəndḗt) 'thumb'.
new_statements.citation: Simeone-Senelle, Marie-Claude. 1997. The Modern South Arabian Languages. In Robert Hetzron (ed.), The Semitic Languages, 378-423. London: Routledge.
new_statements.locator: p. 386, section 'Other Phenomena: Syllabic Structure and Stress' (saved PDF page 407; djvu text lines 24974-24988)
new_statements.rule_in_words: Per this survey: a Jibbali word (or stress unit) may carry more than one stressed syllable; when it carries a single stress, it sits where the Mehri cognate's stress sits, i.e. on the last long syllable, or on the first syllable if every syllable is short. Caveat from other opened sources: Johnstone 1975: 11 says Jibbali vowel length is phonetic and is itself a product of stress (long in stressed open syllables), and Dufour 2017: 192 treats Jibbali stress as distinctive and 'a feature of the pattern' (paroxytone C1V́C2əC3 vs oxytone C1eC2ɛ́C3 templates), so the 'last long syllable' rule is partly circular and the stress position is in practice fixed by the morphological pattern.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Source speaks of 'several stressed syllables' per word (Johnstone 1975: 12 likewise: 'many forms having multiple stress'); Castagna 2024: 52 (citing Dufour 2016: 36) reports a secondary stress on the penultimate CV syllable in yes/no questions, protases and topicalisation.
new_statements.exceptions: Multiple-stress words (JL minšérɔ́t). Johnstone 1975: 12 notes exceptions for forms with a final guttural radical; Castagna 2024: 34 (after al-Kathiri & Dufour 2020: 182) notes /ə/ can never be stressed.
new_statements.domain_note: Word / 'stress unit'; Jibbali examples are citation forms taken from Johnstone's Jibbali Lexicon (JL), whose stress notation al-Kathiri & Dufour 2020: 172 (quoted in Castagna 2024: 218 n. 18) call unreliable for the position of stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Statement covers Jibbali/Śḥeri generally (data from Johnstone's Jibbali Lexicon, i.e. mainly the central/eastern mainland varieties), glottocode sheh1240. Castagna 2018 describes the Kuria Muria (al-Hallaniya) island variety and Castagna 2024 the Eastern (Ṭawi Aʕtair, Sadḥ) varieties; neither gives a stress rule. Bittner 1917 describes the Šḫauri of D. H. von Müller's informants (early 20th c.).

sources.locator: p. 386, section 'Other Phenomena: Syllabic Structure and Stress' (saved PDF page 407; djvu text lines 24974-24988)
sources.note: p. 386 'Syllabic Structure and Stress': Mehri/Hobyot/Bathari/Harsusi stress on the last long syllable, or on the first syllable if all syllables are short; Jibbali can have several stressed syllables in one word/stress unit (JL minšérɔ́t 'middle finger'); when a word has only one stress it is on the same syllable as the Mehri cognate (JL mišəndɔ́t 'thumb'). Jibbali data are cited from Johnstone's Jibbali Lexicon (JL).

sources.citation: Castagna, Giuliano. 2024. An Annotated Corpus of Three Hundred Proverbs, Sayings, and Idioms in Eastern Jibbali/Śḥərɛ̄t. Cambridge: Open Book Publishers. doi:10.11647/OBP.0422
sources.note: Introductory phonology notes (pp. 29-36) give no general stress rule; states /ə/ 'is prosodically lighter than the other vowels and cannot be stressed' (p. 34, citing al-Kathiri & Dufour 2020: 182); a secondary stress on the penultimate CV syllable in yes/no questions, protases and topicalisation (p. 52, citing Dufour 2016: 36); p. 218 n. 18 quotes al-Kathiri & Dufour 2020: 172 that JL's transcription 'often blurs crucial phonological facts, and in particular the position of stress'.

sources.citation: Johnstone, T. M. 1975. The Modern South Arabian Languages. Afroasiatic Linguistics 1/5. Malibu: Undena.
sources.note: §2.2 'The Vowel System and Stress', pp. 10-12 (AAL 1, 102-104). p. 12: 'in the MSA languages the stress regressed to the final syllable wherever there was no pre-final long syllable in a form. Certain exceptions... forms having a final guttural radical'; 'In Ś [Śḥeri = Jibbali] however a contrary tendency has resulted in many forms having multiple stress, the vowels of stressed open syllables being phonetically long, but probably phonologically short.' p. 11: in Ś vowels are long in stressed open syllables and final stressed VC syllables, length 'a phonetic rather than a phonological feature'…

sources.citation: Bittner, Maximilian. 1917 [1915]. Studien zur Šḫauri-Sprache in den Bergen von Dofâr am Persischen Meerbusen. I. Zur Lautlehre und zum Nomen im engeren Sinne. SBAW phil.-hist. Kl. 179/2. Wien: Hölder.
sources.note: §2 'Betonung und Vokalverkürzung', p. 5: 'Das Šḫauri, dessen Betonung im allgemeinen dieselbe ist wie die des Mehri, pflegt nämlich die langen Vokale des Mehri, gleichgiltig ob diese von Haus aus lang sind oder ihre Länge nur dem Akzente verdanken, zu kürzen' (accentuation in general the same as Mehri; Mehri long/stressed vowels shortened). Refers back to his Mehri-Studien for the rules; based on D. H. von Müller's field notes.

sources.citation: Castagna, Giuliano. 2018. A sketch of the Kuria Muria language variety and other aspects of Modern South Arabian. PhD thesis, University of Leeds.
sources.note: Phonology sketch of the Kuria Muria (al-Hallaniya) variety, §3.5.1 pp. 111-135: consonants, vowels, sound shifts; no stress-placement statement. Stress only mentioned as utterance-level prominence conditioning /ḳ/ > [g] (p. 112) and in the literature review of Dufour 2016 (p. 68: 'stress accent rules' shared across MSA).

sources.citation: Kungl, Anton. 2023. Nominal morphophonology of the Modern South Arabian languages. PhD thesis, Nantes Université.
sources.note: Off-target: the analysis is of Omani Mehri nominal patterns (stress 'falls on the second vowel site from the left' in Mehri plurals, p. 15.1.1); no Jibbali stress statement.

sources.citation: Dufour, Julien. 2022. Vowel Quality as a History Maker. Stress, Metaphony and the Renewal of Proto-Semitic Morphology in Modern South Arabian. In P. Epps, D. Law & N. Pat-El (eds), Historical Linguistics and Endangered Languages, 56-96. London: Routledge. doi:10.4324/9780429030390-4
sources.note: Diachronic: Proto-MSA stress was quality-sensitive (selects the rightmost non-final *a over *i/*u; final CV(V)# never stressed; Jibbali more prone than Mehri to stress V0), pp. 56-57, 66-68 with Jibbali tables 4.7-4.9; modern MSA languages 'do not exhibit quality-sensitive stress in their modern forms' and word stress is now fixed (p. 57). No synchronic placement rule for Jibbali.

sources.citation: Klimiuk, Maciej (ed.). 2022. Semitic Dialects and Dialectology: Fieldwork—Community—Change. Heidelberg: heiUP (incl. Castagna, A Text in the Jibbali/Shehret Dialect of al-Hallaniya, pp. 245ff.).
sources.note: Nothing on stress in the Jibbali contribution.

sources.citation: Dufour, Julien. 2017. Nouns and adjectives of the shape C1V́C2(ə)C3(-) in Jibbali (Śħri) and Mehri. Brill's Journal of Afroasiatic Languages and Linguistics 9: 191-217. doi:10.1163/18776930-00901009
sources.note: p. 192: 'Jibbali and Mehri have distinctive word stress, and stress can be considered a feature of the pattern.' §2.1.1 (p. 194): Johnstone usually does not write stress on monosyllables; §5.2 (pp. 214-215): stress position differs by pattern, e.g. paroxytone C1éC2əC3 (< *C1aC2iC3) vs oxytone C1eC2ɛ́C3 (bedɛ́n 'body' < *C1aC2aC3); n. 14 contrasts paroxytones (bɛ́ḳəl, ˁáḳər) with oxytones (ðelɛ́b, geðɛ́m, helɛ́k). No surface placement rule; stress treated as lexically/morphologically fixed.
